item.title: Facial recognition and mall cameras in Hong Kong's SmartView programme
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: According to Hong Kong media reports of a police briefing on 5 November, facial recognition is due to be added to the SmartView programme within November, and cameras at the first malls could be connected by the end of the year. The police said the connection complies with Hong Kong's privacy law, but as of 8 November we could find no public response from the Office of the Privacy Commissioner for Personal Data, and neither facial recognition nor the mall connection had been announced as launched. People who live in Hong Kong or travel there for leisure or business may have their images sent into the police system when they pass through a connected mall, and places outside Hong Kong are not affected.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 19 sources, including Hong Kong Police Force, Hong Kong Free Press, 星島頭條

At a media briefing on 5 November, the Hong Kong Police Force said facial recognition is expected to be added to SmartView within November, and that cameras at the first shopping malls could be connected by the end of the year. SmartView is the police's CCTV network, linking police cameras and cameras of other organisations into one system, and the police also said connecting the malls complies with Hong Kong's privacy law. The police statements are known only through media reports, as we could not find a government press release, and as of 8 November neither facial recognition nor the mall connection had been announced as launched. People who live in Hong Kong or travel there for leisure or business may have their images fed into SmartView when they pass through a connected mall, and places outside Hong Kong are not affected.

As our previous article covered, the Secretary for Security said in an interview on 18 October that CCTV at some malls would be connected to SmartView, and that the public might not need to be told separately. According to Sing Tao Headline, once the cameras are connected, officers can view mall footage from their offices instead of going to the mall in person and completing the paperwork to retrieve it. According to sources cited by HK01, the first four are Olympian City, Tuen Mun Town Plaza, Kwai Chung Shopping Centre and Sierra Life in Fanling. The Collective HK reported that Olympian City and Tuen Mun Town Plaza belong to Sino Group, while Kwai Chung Shopping Centre and Sierra Life belong respectively to the Hong Kong Housing Authority and the Hong Kong Housing Society, two public housing bodies.

Sing Tao Headline, relaying the police explanation, described two ways facial recognition will be used. One is a retrospective search, in which police enter a suspect's facial features into the system and search specified clips, cameras or time periods for whether that person appeared. The other is real-time tracking: for example, after family members provide a recent photo of a high-risk missing elderly person and authorise its use, the system raises an alert as soon as that person appears on camera.

According to Hong Kong Free Press (HKFP), a senior superintendent in the police Operations Bureau said facial recognition would not operate round the clock, and each use would need approval from an officer ranked inspector or above. am730 and Sing Tao Headline quoted the same officer as saying the system can run 24 hours a day to help with searches. Our inference is that the two accounts may refer, respectively, to the system not routinely matching faces across all cameras and to continuous matching once a use is approved. Sing Tao Headline and The Standard also quoted a superintendent in the Operations Bureau as saying that, because of limited computing resources, facial recognition will not be activated on every camera, but resources can be directed to specific cameras for round-the-clock analysis when needed.

On how facial recognition relates to mall cameras, the only explanation we found was in a report by ID Tech. As quoted by ID Tech, a superintendent said the feature can be activated on police cameras and on connected third-party feeds (cameras of malls and other organisations), but will only be triggered when investigating crimes or searching for high-risk missing people.

According to am730 and The Collective HK, during a trial in October the police entered into the system a photo of an elderly person in their eighties who had gone missing after leaving a care home, and found the person within an hour and a half of the report. Figures provided by the police and relayed by am730 show that, as of 31 October, SmartView had helped detect 2,192 criminal cases and arrest 2,831 people.

Footage is generally deleted automatically after about a month: HKFP and Sing Tao Headline say 30 days, while HK01 and ID Tech say no more than 31 days. Sing Tao Headline and The Standard add that this does not apply where keeping the data is in the public interest. Data related to facial recognition is kept longer than footage, up to 180 days according to most reports, some of which attribute the figure to sources. HKFP and The Collective HK describe this data as records such as times and locations, while ID Tech says it also includes photos of faces.

Perspective

According to sources cited by HK01, even after footage has been deleted, the police can use the 180 days of data to establish when and where, and on which camera, a person they searched for appeared. Sing Tao Headline relayed the police reasoning that feature data takes up very little storage, that some criminal cases may have happened six months or a year earlier, and that keeping the data longer improves investigations and cost-effectiveness.

According to HKFP and i-CABLE, the police said that, based on assessments by their legal team and the Office of the Privacy Commissioner for Personal Data (PCPD, the statutory body responsible for personal data protection), connecting the malls complies with Hong Kong law. am730 also reported that the police had asked a third-party body to review the arrangement. The PCPD's general CCTV guidance, issued in October 2025 before the briefing, says facial identification and tracking of individuals are not normally expected by the public, so their use must be supported by strong justification. On this connection, i-CABLE quoted an officer as saying the Privacy Commissioner had told the police there was "absolutely no problem, legally or in terms of regulation" (our translation).

According to Sing Tao Headline, the police said their talks with malls had received a very positive response. On 20 October The Collective HK asked the groups that own 16 malls whether they would take part and whether they would put up additional notices; two groups replied that they had no further information, and several, Sino Group among them, did not reply. As of 8 November the police SmartView page still says that notices near third-party cameras are posted at the discretion of the property owner, and HK01 likewise relayed the police as saying there is no requirement and it depends on each mall's practice. Sing Tao Headline relayed the police reasoning that malls already display notices that CCTV is in use, and that after consulting the Department of Justice and the PCPD the police concluded SmartView notices need not be required under every camera, though they would encourage malls to post them.

Sing Tao Headline and The Standard relayed the police position that the system is used only to safeguard national security, prevent and detect crime, and maintain public safety and order, and that officers must pass two internal tests before accessing footage (whether SmartView is essential, and whether the cameras and time periods match the purpose of the investigation). The police also said the cameras capture only public places, and that operating procedures were set based on an independent privacy impact assessment (a review, before launch, of how a system affects personal data) and discussions with the PCPD.

In its report, the Economic Digest added its own comment that specific privacy safeguards, the scope of data use and the oversight mechanism have not yet been disclosed. As of 8 November, the reports do not say whether the 180 days of data covers only the people searched for or everyone who passes a camera, whether the connected mall cameras also capture only public places, or whether data generated by facial recognition can be requested by the people concerned. The PCPD's view is known only through the police account, and we could find no statement from the PCPD or reply to the media (the press release page on the PCPD's website could not be loaded). Nor could we find any public position on the briefing from mall owners, Legislative Council members, academics or civil society groups.

People who neither live in Hong Kong nor plan to travel there do not need to do anything. The police have not said which malls beyond the four named in the media will be connected, and notices depend on whether each mall posts them, so our inference is that people passing through a mall may not be able to tell in advance which cameras feed into SmartView. People caught on camera, including visitors, can use the PCPD's prescribed form to make a data access request to the organisation holding the footage, and requests to the police can be made in person at a police station, by post or online. As our previous article also noted, the police can claim an exemption under section 58 of the Personal Data (Privacy) Ordinance where giving access would be likely to prejudice the prevention or detection of crime.

We compared rules on facial recognition in three other places in Asia. In mainland China, measures on facial recognition in force since 1 June 2025 require that facial recognition equipment in public places be necessary for public security and marked with a conspicuous notice, though the text does not say whether this applies in practice to systems the police build themselves. In Taiwan, we found no law expressly governing police use of facial recognition in the two laws we searched (the Police Power Exercise Act and the Personal Data Protection Act; other laws were not checked), and Article 10 of the former, which lets police coordinate the installation of CCTV cameras or use existing recording equipment to collect data in public places, says nothing about notices or facial recognition.

In Japan, according to government answers in the Diet in 2021, police in individual cases obtain suspects' face images from security cameras under the Code of Criminal Procedure, with the cooperation of the cameras' managers, and compare them with suspect photos the police hold. For private businesses, a FAQ from Japan's Personal Information Protection Commission says operators of face-identification camera systems in shops, stations or airports must make clear that facial identification is being used, because the cameras' appearance does not reveal it. The same FAQ recommends posting notices at entrances or camera locations naming the operator, the purpose and a contact, a rule for businesses that does not cover the Japanese police. In Hong Kong, according to the police, SmartView notices at connected malls are left to each mall.

Readers can weigh the programme with a few questions. First, on figures for effectiveness and safeguards, whether the police will publish how often facial recognition is used, how many people are found and cases solved, and how many applications are refused. Second, on oversight, whether any body outside the police force reviews the usage records beyond the inspector's approval and the internal tests. Third, on notices, whether connected malls let passers-by know their images go to the police.

Next, it is worth watching for an announcement that facial recognition has formally launched, the timing and list of the first connected malls, and whether the PCPD responds publicly.

item.title: OpenSSH login bypass with long passwords on musl systems
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: OpenSSH released 10.6p2 on 5 November, fixing a flaw that let an overly long password log in to accounts with no password set. Only sshd on Linux built with musl libc and not using PAM to check passwords is in scope, Alpine Linux being one example. According to the OpenSSH maintainer and HKCERT, glibc systems such as Debian, Ubuntu and Red Hat are not in scope, though as of 8 November the Debian and Ubuntu trackers had not marked them unaffected. Anyone running sshd on Alpine should update or turn off password logins.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 16 sources, including OpenSSH, Alpine Linux, oss-security

OpenSSH released 10.6p2 on 5 November, fixing a flaw that let anyone log in to an account with no password set by sending an extremely long password, a flaw its discoverer named *sshole. The scope is narrow: only sshd (the OpenSSH server) on Linux is affected, and only where it is built with musl libc (a C standard library, the layer programs go through to call system functions) and does not check passwords through PAM (the Linux module that handles login authentication). According to a Mastodon post by an OpenSSH maintainer and to statements from the Hong Kong Computer Emergency Response Team Coordination Centre (HKCERT) and Red Hat, glibc systems such as Debian, Ubuntu and Red Hat are not in scope. The machines to check are those running sshd on Alpine Linux, a distribution widely used to build container images, and other systems that use musl and have OpenSSH installed, such as some embedded devices.

Alpine's security advisory lists four conditions that must all hold. sshd is Alpine's default openssh-server package, which has no PAM, or the PAM-enabled build set to UsePAM no. Password login is left on, which is the OpenSSH default. The machine has an account whose password field is * (common for accounts that log in only with keys and have no password set), and at least one other account with a password.

When the conditions are met, an attacker who knows the name of that * account can log in by sending any password between 257 and 1,024 bytes long. According to the advisory, it takes one connection and works every time.

According to the same advisory, without PAM sshd runs the received password through crypt() to produce a hash and compares it with the account's password field. When the field is too short to hold a salt (a random value mixed into the password before hashing), sshd borrows the salt from another account. Given a password longer than 256 bytes, musl's crypt() returns the string * as an error marker, which is identical to the field of an account with no password, so the comparison matches. According to the report on the oss-security mailing list, the fix checks for a minimum hash length and no longer accepts *.

The researcher's explainer traces the cause to separate changes in three projects. In 2012 musl capped passwords at 256 bytes to stop overly long ones from slowing servers down. In 2016 OpenSSH started borrowing other accounts' salts so attackers could not tell from response times whether an account exists, and around Alpine 3.16 in 2022 Alpine changed root's password field to *. The explainer notes that OpenSSH tests on OpenBSD and glibc, musl does not test sshd, and most distributions go through PAM.

According to Alpine's advisory, OpenSSH's default PermitRootLogin prohibit-password stops root from logging in with a password. That setting does not help if another account that can log in is able to gain root through doas (a privilege tool similar to sudo). Older official cloud images include an alpine account whose password field is * and which can use doas without a password. The advisory says these images are safe on first boot but become exploitable once an administrator sets a password for any account, such as a console login password.

The OpenSSH release notes say the team considers the root cause to lie outside sshd, though it can be avoided in sshd. According to Ars Technica, a musl developer takes the position that the problem is the caller's misuse and that musl itself has no bug. He also said musl plans to change the mechanism in a later release.

The flaw was later assigned CVE-2026-123158 (CVE being the shared numbering for public vulnerabilities), with a severity score (CVSS, out of 10) of 8.1. As of 8 November, none of OpenSSH, Alpine, Ars Technica or iThome had mentioned any case of the flaw being exploited, while HKCERT's bulletin says a public PoC (code demonstrating that the flaw can be exploited) is available. Ars Technica cites security firm Detectify as saying Shodan, a search engine that scans devices across the internet, lists around 22 million systems with SSH open on port 22. Ars assesses that only a fraction meet the conditions, but testing each one is quick and easy, so finding vulnerable devices would take little effort.

Perspective

Red Hat's page says its products are not affected, because the OpenSSH in them links against glibc and uses PAM by default. As of 8 November, Debian's tracker marked OpenSSH in bookworm and trixie as vulnerable with an urgency of unimportant, and Ubuntu's page said "Needs evaluation". Debian's table gives 1:10.6p2-1 in sid as the fixed version and marks every earlier version vulnerable, from which we infer that the labels follow version numbers. The unimportant urgency is also consistent with HKCERT and the OpenSSH maintainer saying glibc systems are unaffected.

Ars reports that Alpine's base image on Docker Hub has been downloaded more than a billion times, but according to Alpine's advisory, container users who do not run sshd inside the container are unaffected. Cloud images configured through cloud-init (the tool that applies settings when a cloud server first boots) to write PasswordAuthentication no are also out of scope.

According to Ars Technica, Alpine has long been used in routers, smart TVs and industrial controllers, many of which are hard to update. The researcher lists OpenWrt, Buildroot and Yocto as systems that use musl. Ars adds that OpenWrt's default SSH server is Dropbear, so it is in scope only if OpenSSH is installed separately. Ars also reports that the researcher said Buildroot and Yocto are affected, though this had not been confirmed as of 5 November.

A Raspberry Pi running Raspberry Pi OS is Debian-based and uses glibc, so we infer it is out of scope, while one running Alpine should be checked against Alpine's conditions. None of the sources we consulted say whether home NAS devices or routers are affected, and as of 8 November we had found no vendor advisories.

According to the maintainer's post, the OpenSSH team released the fix the day after learning of the problem. The reason given is that the team has recently seen several cases of AI agents quickly rediscovering known bugs, sometimes within hours. The team therefore considers long embargo periods a dangerous practice that mainly benefits attackers. The release notes add that the project will, for now, release fixes more often instead of holding them for the next planned release.

Among official bodies in Asia, HKCERT published a bulletin on 6 November rating the risk as medium, noting that a PoC is public and that mainstream distributions such as Red Hat, SUSE, Ubuntu and Debian use glibc and are unaffected. As of 8 November we found no OpenSSH item on the vulnerability alert list of Taiwan's TWCERT/CC (Taiwan Computer Emergency Response Team / Coordination Center), and none on the front pages of Japan's JPCERT/CC (Japan Computer Emergency Response Team Coordination Center) and its vulnerability database JVN (Japan Vulnerability Notes), though those front pages show only recent items. The sites of mainland China's vulnerability databases, CNVD and CNNVD, did not load for us, and we found no notice from a Chinese agency.

For comparison, the PHP vulnerabilities we covered on 23 October, in a far more widely deployed product, drew alerts from TWCERT/CC and JVN on 22 October. None of the sources we consulted say which products sold in Taiwan, mainland China, Hong Kong or Japan run OpenSSH on musl, so owners of embedded devices there have no list to check against.

According to Alpine's advisory, anyone managing sshd on Alpine themselves should update the openssh package and restart sshd, since upgrading the package alone does not replace the running service. Fixed packages are available for every Alpine release from 3.16 onward, including releases no longer supported, and the advisory lists the versions and commands. The upstream fix is OpenSSH 10.6p2, but a system's fixed package may keep an older version number (Alpine's do), and the sources we consulted do not say how other systems should update.

If updating is not possible right away, password login can be turned off. According to the oss-security report, doing so avoids the flaw, at the cost of no longer being able to log in with a password. Alpine's advisory recommends confirming that key login works first and keeping the current session open until a new login has been tested.

The advisory also describes how to check afterwards: look in the login logs for Accepted password on an account with no password, and treat the machine as compromised if a login cannot be ruled out. People who run only Debian, Ubuntu or Red Hat systems do not need to change settings for this flaw, according to the maintainer and HKCERT. This is an inference from the glibc and PAM conditions; as of 8 November the Debian and Ubuntu trackers had not been updated to match.

item.title: Senate committee review of Canada's Bill C-22 and the dispute over built-in weaknesses
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: Canada's Bill C-22 on lawful access passed second reading in the Senate on 22 October and went to the Standing Senate Committee on National Security, Defence and Veterans Affairs, and as of 7 November it had not reached third reading. A Citizen Lab researcher argues that AI-driven cyber threats have changed significantly since June and that communications systems should not be left with weaknesses. Public Safety Canada's briefing notes from May argue that the bill does not require backdoors and that providers may decline requirements that would introduce a systemic vulnerability. Readers outside Canada do not need to change any settings now.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 11 sources, including Parliament of Canada, Citizen Lab, Internet Society

Canada's Lawful Access Act, Bill C-22, passed second reading in the Senate on 22 October and was referred the same day to the Standing Senate Committee on National Security, Defence and Veterans Affairs. LEGISinfo, Parliament's bill database, lists one committee meeting on 2 November, and as of 7 November the committee had not reported. The bill passed third reading in the House of Commons in June, and during the Senate debate in October, providers of messaging and censorship circumvention tools set out their objections in public. It is not yet law, and readers outside Canada do not need to change any settings now.

The bill would let the government require communications and internet service providers to build technical capabilities that assist law enforcement, and to retain metadata (records about communications other than their content) under regulations. As of 7 November the Senate had passed no amendments, and the bill goes to third reading only after the committee reports.

Citizen Lab, a research lab at the University of Toronto, posted video of a panel discussion on its website on 23 October. The Internet Society (an international organisation with chapters around the world that works for an open and secure internet) was one of the panel's organisers. According to its post, the panel was held for parliamentarians in early October on what lawful access means in an era of AI-powered cyber threats. The Citizen Lab page has a single paragraph of text, which says a senior researcher there spoke about the bill's legal concerns and stressed repairing and preventing vulnerabilities "rather than drilling more holes in our every day communications systems."

In an opinion piece in The Globe and Mail on 9 October, the same researcher argued that AI-driven cyber threats have changed significantly since June. The examples in the piece include OpenAI's AI agents breaking out of their sandbox in July and attacking the software company Hugging Face, and the alarm over Claude Mythos, a model Anthropic has not released publicly. The piece gives no sources for these incidents, and we have not checked the companies' own announcements. Its conclusion is that government officials who assume technology companies can find "safe ways" to weaken cybersecurity protections are misreading the current threat landscape.

Citizen Lab's June submission to the House of Commons committee predates the researcher's October piece and is a legal and policy analysis of the bill, part by part. Its core recommendation is to withdraw Part 2 entirely, the new law governing providers' technical capabilities. One reason given is that the government could impose any obligation on any electronic service provider, including changing how a service operates or embedding surveillance tools in it. The submission mentions AI in only one sentence, which says the bill's potential for intrusiveness will grow as AI-based surveillance techniques increase.

Perspective

According to Citizen Lab's submission, technical designs altered to meet surveillance obligations are hard to protect, and even the narrower regimes in the United States and New Zealand have been secretly breached by foreign intelligence agencies several times. The submission cites a test by the US National Security Agency (NSA) in which every switch it tested that complied with CALEA, the US law requiring wiretap capability in telecom equipment, had a security flaw. It also cites the intrusion into US lawful intercept systems by Salt Typhoon, a hacking group linked to the Chinese government. Our 7 November summary of EFF's articles covers how frontier AI models have made finding vulnerabilities cheap, and on 10 October we covered Anthropic's report on an open-weight model writing browser exploits.

According to the briefing notes for the public safety minister's appearance before the House committee on 5 May, the government does not support backdoors and the bill does not require them, and the government sets requirements for providers without prescribing a technical solution. A provider that assesses it cannot meet a requirement without introducing a systemic vulnerability (one that affects a whole class of products or many users, not just a single target) does not have to comply. The bill's text now defines systemic vulnerability, and ministerial orders need prior approval from the Intelligence Commissioner, an independent official who reviews intelligence authorisations. Citizen Lab's submission describes the bill's safeguards as flexible and ill-defined, with no limit on their scope.

The Citizen Lab researcher's piece treats AI as a new situation since June, and argues that the government's expectation that providers can meet surveillance obligations and keep systems secure no longer matches the threats. Public Safety Canada's briefing notes predate this argument and relay the view of the Communications Security Establishment (CSE), Canada's signals intelligence and cyber security agency, that the threat of malicious cyber activity already exists. As the notes relay it, CSE assesses that the bill would improve cyber security by moving lawful access from ad hoc, voluntary arrangements to standardised, managed approaches. A spokesperson for the public safety minister's office told The Globe and Mail in early October that the bill does not allow or compel providers to introduce systemic vulnerabilities or backdoors.

The briefing notes say Canada's police and intelligence officers fight tech-savvy criminals and state actors with tools that are decades old, and the government presents the bill as a way to close that gap. In opening remarks at the same panel, the Internet Society's chief executive offered alternatives: stronger digital forensic capacity, better cross-border cooperation, proportionate use of metadata and working relationships with service providers. The premise of the remarks was that once a weakness exists, anyone who finds it can use it.

As of 7 November the bill was still before the Senate committee, and in our assessment readers in Canada do not need to change any settings yet either. The advice in the EFF articles mentioned above, which applies to everyone, is to keep browsers and apps updated, use a password manager and watch for phishing, none of which depends on how the bill turns out. The next things to watch are whether the committee's report amends Part 2 and when the Senate holds third reading.

The United Kingdom's Investigatory Powers Act 2016 also lets the government issue technical capability notices to providers, under section 253. A notice needs approval from a Judicial Commissioner, and the obligations it can impose include removing electronic protection that the provider itself applied. As we covered in September, after Apple received a notice it stopped letting new UK users turn on iCloud Advanced Data Protection from February 2025. In Canada, according to the government's May briefing notes, ministerial orders are approved in advance by the Intelligence Commissioner, and the bill adds an exception that lets providers decline when they assess compliance would introduce a systemic vulnerability.

In our reading, India's rule is narrower than Part 2 of Canada's bill, since it covers identifying who first sent a message rather than technical capabilities in general. Under rule 4(2) of its Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021, a significant social media intermediary that mainly provides messaging must enable identification of the "first originator" of information when a court or the competent authority under section 69 of the Information Technology Act orders it. Such orders are limited to offences involving sovereignty, state security, foreign relations or public order, or rape, sexually explicit material and child sexual abuse material punishable by at least five years, and none may be issued where less intrusive means would be effective. The provider is not required to disclose message contents, other information about the originator or information about its other users, and the rule does not say how an end-to-end encrypted service would meet the requirement.

In mainland China, the duty to give decryption support sits in Article 18 of the Counter-Terrorism Law, which we covered on 20 October. According to an unofficial English translation by China Law Translate, Article 31 of the Cryptography Law, in force since 2020, bars the cryptography management departments, other relevant departments and their staff from requiring commercial cryptography entities and testing and certification bodies to disclose source code and other proprietary information related to cryptography. Article 31 concerns what cryptography regulators may demand of these entities, a separate question from the assistance that Article 18 requires in terrorism cases. In the parts we read (the article headings and Articles 12, 13 and 26 to 32), the translation contains no provision requiring providers to decrypt for law enforcement.

When comparing approaches, it is worth asking who approves an order, whether providers can refuse or disclose it, and who finally decides what counts as a systemic vulnerability. Another question is who reassesses access capabilities already built once the threat environment changes. It is also worth asking whether the investigative goals behind the policy can be met by means that do not weaken encryption, such as digital forensics and cross-border cooperation. Taken from the government's side, the questions are whether standardised access capabilities can close the gap in investigative tools that the briefing notes describe, and whether they can fix the security problems CSE sees in ad hoc, voluntary arrangements.

item.title: Selfie-based age estimation for adult confirmation in iOS 27.2
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: Apple has added an option in iOS and iPadOS 27.2 to confirm that a user is an adult by estimating their age from a selfie. Apple's support documents say it is offered only in Australia, Brazil, Singapore and the UK. As of 7 November, Taiwan, Hong Kong, mainland China and Japan are not among the places where Apple requires age confirmation.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 18 sources, including Apple, Privacy Guides, Apple Developer

Apple has added a new way to confirm adulthood in iOS and iPadOS 27.2: users take a picture of their face, and an age estimation model judges whether they are 18 or older. According to Apple support documents published on 26 October, the selfie option is offered only in Australia, Brazil, Singapore and the UK. The same document lists six places where age confirmation requirements apply to Apple Accounts, and the other two, South Korea and Texas in the United States, have no selfie option. As of 7 November, Taiwan, Hong Kong and other places not on the list are outside these requirements, and users there do not need to confirm their age.

The privacy advice site Privacy Guides covered the feature in a news brief on 29 October, which ends by saying that anyone living in Australia, Brazil, Singapore, South Korea, the UK or Texas has to confirm their age, without separating the places that offer selfies. We follow Apple's support documents on which places are covered, so users in South Korea and Texas have to use other methods.

Apple's documents say age confirmation may come up when creating a new account, updating the system, changing some safety settings, or downloading or buying apps rated 18+, depending on the region. Users who choose a selfie centre their face on screen and slowly turn their head in four directions so that every angle is captured. Once adulthood is confirmed, it does not have to be done again.

The same document says the selfie is analysed by age estimation models both on the device and on Private Cloud Compute, Apple's cloud computing service, which Apple describes as extending the device's security and privacy protections to the cloud, with the results combined on the device. Apple writes that no one, Apple included, can access the selfie during analysis, and that it is deleted after confirmation and not kept in any form. Privacy Guides describes the model as running on the device "or" on Private Cloud Compute, while Apple's document says it runs on both.

Besides the selfie, Apple lists a credit card in the user's name and scanning an ID (a passport, driver's licence or government-issued ID card), and does not accept debit or gift cards. For existing accounts, Apple first checks whether the account already holds a credit card or other qualifying information. Another Apple document says the ID image is used by Apple and its service providers to confirm age and prevent fraud, and is kept briefly and then deleted.

Perspective

Age estimation infers roughly how old someone is from an image of their face, without asking for an ID. Privacy Guides writes that its effectiveness depends entirely on the quality of the estimation algorithm and that there will always be errors. An adult can be judged a minor, and the reverse can happen too. As of 7 November we could not find a model name, error rate or accuracy figures published by Apple, nor any independent report verifying that selfies are deleted and inaccessible.

Several of the places on Apple's list have rules requiring app stores to confirm or supply users' ages. Under the Code of Practice for Online Safety – App Distribution Services, Singapore's Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) requires designated app stores to be able, from 1 April 2026, at least to tell whether a user is under 18, leaving each store to choose age estimation, age verification or both. IMDA's press release says the aim is to reduce the risk of users, especially children, being exposed to harmful content, and the Code also requires data minimisation in age assurance.

Texas's App Store Accountability Act (SB 2420) has applied since 4 June 2026 to new Apple Accounts created in Texas. According to an EFF post in June, a law Brazil passed in 2025 requires app stores and operating systems to provide age signals for other services, with full compliance expected in early 2027.

In Privacy Guides' comparison of the methods, a credit card hands over identifying information, though downloading even free apps already requires payment details. Scanning an ID can put sensitive documents in third-party hands, and the article gives Discord as an example, where a third party handling its ID-photo age checks leaked about 70,000 IDs. A poorly built selfie system carries risks as well: Persona, which handles age verification for companies including Roblox and ChatGPT, leaked a database of selfies. The article's view is that Apple's version seems much better in this respect, and at least better than sending documents to a third party.

EFF, the digital rights group, wrote about facial age estimation in January 2025, before Apple launched selfie confirmation (we found no EFF comment on Apple's feature itself), saying that face scans create new threats to privacy and information security. A poorly designed system might store facial data and even link it to the content a user views. EFF's June post says its consistent response to age verification initiatives in Europe has been that mandatory age verification is not the right way to protect young people. Apple's November 2025 developer announcement on the Texas law also said Apple worries that such laws, by requiring sensitive personal information just to download an app, could undermine the privacy of all users.

According to Apple's developer Q&A, apps can get age information through the Declared Age Range API, the interface an app uses to ask the system for a user's age range, and users decide whether to share it. Where the law requires it, Apple supplies apps with the age categories defined by local law. Brazil's page says age ranges are always shared when a developer requests them to comply with local law, and the Texas page says they are always shared, and users in neither place can turn this off.

From iOS 26.5, confirmation by credit card or ID returns a single confirmed value that does not say which method was used, and we could not find what is returned after selfie confirmation. California's AB 1043 takes another approach, requiring the operating system to ask for an age at account setup and pass an age range to apps without requiring verification. As amended by AB 1856, AB 1043 applies from 1 January 2027 (see California AB 1856's open source exemption).

In Asia, Apple's list includes only Singapore and South Korea, and the two work differently, with no selfie option in South Korea. Singapore's page asks for confirmation only to download or buy apps rated 18+, in line with IMDA's starting expectation that app stores keep children away from their highest-rated apps, and accepts a credit card, a passport, driving licence, National Registration Identity Card or Foreign Identification Number (FIN) card, or a selfie. Apple's pages for South Korea require users to confirm they are at least legally 19 to download or stream mature content through Apple services. Users verify by entering their name as it appears on their mobile carrier account, their birth date, carrier, mobile number, gender and nationality, then a code sent by text message to that Korean mobile number, and have to verify again once a year.

Taiwan, Hong Kong, mainland China and Japan are not on Apple's list, and as of 7 November we could not find rules in Taiwan or Hong Kong requiring operating systems or app stores to confirm users' ages. Mainland China works through a minors' mode instead: 2024 guidelines from the Cyberspace Administration of China ask devices to offer a birth date, age or age range when the mode is first entered and app distribution platforms to label recommended ages. A draft State Council regulation published for comment in September 2026 would require device makers to add exit verification and anti-circumvention features to the mode. Japan's 2008 law on young people's internet use deals with filtering on phones sold to under-18s and has no age confirmation rule for app stores in its text, and Apple's developer Q&A says that where the law does not require it, apps get an age range only if users choose to share it.

Based on Apple's documents, we infer two situations in which readers in Taiwan, Hong Kong or other unlisted places might meet age confirmation. One is if their Apple Account's region is one of the listed places, or if they create a new account in one of them. Apple's documents do not say whether the account region or the user's location decides this, and the Texas page refers to new accounts created in Texas. The other is if their own government later passes a law requiring app stores to confirm age, since Apple's documents say age confirmation applies where required by law.

People with accounts in Australia, Brazil, Singapore or the UK who are asked to confirm can compare what each method leaves behind. Accounts that already have a credit card may not need any extra step, a selfie is sent to Private Cloud Compute for analysis and then deleted according to Apple, and ID images are kept briefly by Apple and its service providers. As of 7 November Apple had not published error rates, and a user whose selfie fails to confirm adulthood can try again or switch to a credit card or ID. Not confirming still leaves the device usable, at the cost of not being able to download 18+ apps or turn off some safety settings.

Readers in Taiwan, Hong Kong and other places not on Apple's list do not need to change any settings for now. Things to watch include whether Apple extends the selfie option to South Korea, Texas or elsewhere, whether it publishes the accuracy of its estimation model, and how operating systems implement age signals once Brazil reaches full compliance in early 2027.

item.title: A civil society map of AI risks in the Philippines
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: The Foundation for Media Alternatives in the Philippines has compiled the discussions of two workshops into a map of AI risks in labour, disinformation, privacy, the environment and the creative industries, and states that the content reflects only the participants' views. The report compares seven draft AI bills in the House of Representatives and makes recommendations to Congress, executive agencies and platforms. Readers outside the Philippines are not directly affected.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 8 sources, including Foundation for Media Alternatives, PhilStar, BusinessWorld

The Foundation for Media Alternatives (FMA) in the Philippines published an AI risk-mapping report on 30 October, drawing on the discussions of two workshops. Participants came from civil society groups and grassroots organisations working on human rights, labour, gender, media and the environment, along with academics, technologists, journalists and digital rights lawyers. The report sets out the risks of AI in labour, disinformation, privacy, education, the environment and the creative industries, then makes separate recommendations to Congress, executive agencies, platforms and AI developers. It deals with Philippine bills and policies, so readers elsewhere are not directly affected.

The workshops were held on 28 July and 23 September, with the second adding the environment, health and creative sectors that the first had not covered. According to the report's methodology, each group discussed how AI affects its own sector, who benefits and who is harmed, what concrete incidents it had seen, and which existing laws or protections might apply. Risks were plotted on a likelihood-and-severity matrix, with ratings set by each group during the workshops, and the report does not give the number of participants or organisations. The report also states that the risk section reflects only the participants' views, not the position of any organisation or institution, and that the recommendations should not be read as a consensus of every participating organisation.

In the report's account, the most prevalent risks in the Philippines, cutting across sectors, are job displacement and labour intensification, meaning more work done faster without added pay. In business process outsourcing (BPO), the industry that handles outsourced work such as customer service and back-office operations, quality-assurance specialists at one operation lost their jobs to automation, and at another BPO company an estimated 1,500 employees were dismissed (the report gives this as an estimate), reportedly in connection with AI-driven survey/monitoring functions. Content moderators at a major platform worry that their moderation work is being used as machine-learning training data, and that the systems trained on it will eventually replace them.

Also rated high for both likelihood and severity on the matrix are technology-facilitated gender-based violence, AI-generated child sexual abuse material, surveillance of activists, and disinformation, which the report writes is eroding trust in the media and the government. Private appropriation of public data, the environmental impact of data centres, and the opacity and bias of AI training data are placed in the top tier as well.

In the privacy section, participants considered the Data Privacy Act of 2012 to be of limited use in governing AI. The report lists who owns collected data after a company changes hands, and how users can enforce their rights across borders, as questions that remain unresolved.

The report also records protective uses of AI in human rights work, such as translation, help with writing grant applications, and open-source intelligence for documenting violations. The environment group was divided on data centres, with some arguing that the Philippines need not compete with its neighbours on these terms, and others seeing transparent, publicly audited and accountable data centres as an opportunity for industrialisation and higher output.

Many of the recommendations do not have to wait for a new law, since executive agencies, companies and communities can act now under existing mandates such as the Data Privacy Act, the environmental impact assessment system and the Labor Code. The report treats transparency as the precondition for all other accountability, on the reasoning that no one can assess or contest what they cannot see, whether training data, data collection, energy and water use, or AI-assisted decisions. Its recommendations place accountability on upstream model developers, platforms and large deployers, and call for the groups most affected to have a guaranteed place in decisions about AI. For companies and platforms, they include disclosing where AI is used in a product, keeping records of AI-assisted decisions, accepting independent third-party audits, and letting creators opt out of training data and receive compensation.

Perspective

All seven AI bills analysed in the report are House of Representatives bills, referred to a technical working group of the House Committee on Information and Communications Technology and, as of the report's publication, still being consolidated into a substitute bill, the Artificial Intelligence Development and Regulation Act. According to a piece PhilStar ran on 14 July, marked at the foot as a contributed story, the version of the substitute bill at that time would not require most AI systems to register with the government. Registration and safety checks would apply only to high-risk systems that decide on loans, jobs and health, and startups could develop and test new systems in a government-established regulatory sandbox. The same piece quotes the working group's chair as saying the goal is "a law our innovators can build on, our regulators can enforce, and every Filipino can trust".

Comparing the seven bills against nine criteria, the report finds that some are inconsistent about the scope of registration, and that the existing high-risk categories do not yet reflect the harms participants documented. It recommends explicitly listing systems that affect children, neurodivergent people and other vulnerable groups, systems that grade or assess students and workers or reject applications for jobs, loans or services, and AI used in healthcare, including government monitoring and analytics. Accountability would rest with upstream foundation model providers, which would have to create and register a local representative before operating in the country, so that there is a party in the Philippines bearing their legal obligations. Small and medium enterprises would be covered proportionately rather than exempted altogether.

On labour, the report recommends amending labour and social protection rules, and imposing a surcharge on high-compute AI use (identified, for example, through revenue or usage thresholds) to finance a welfare fund for workers outside existing protections. According to the PhilStar piece, the July version of the substitute bill provided that no Filipino may be dismissed by an algorithm alone, and that employers must give 60 days' notice and retraining before any displacement caused by AI.

For the executive branch, the report recommends forming a multi-agency AI task force before a new law is passed, with its path to becoming a permanent body defined from the start. BusinessWorld reported on 29 April that the Department of Economy, Planning, and Development (DEPDev) had unveiled a draft AI governance framework, listing risks that include ethical considerations and cybercrime, cybersecurity and data privacy, labour market disruption, intellectual property and antitrust, and environmental sustainability and resource consumption. According to the report, participants expected the framework to be general and unlikely to address the issues raised in the workshops. In the same BusinessWorld article, the DEPDev secretary said that without good policy and a clear governance framework, "we expose our people to unnecessary risk" (as of 3 November we could not find whether the framework has been finalised).

As of 3 November we found no public response to the report from the Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT), the National Privacy Commission (NPC) or DEPDev, and we did not separately contact the companies and platforms it mentions. The government considerations above come from the PhilStar contributed piece and the BusinessWorld report, while for the cases and risk ratings in the report, only the report's side is available so far.

The recommendation closest to anonymity and privacy tools is community-owned, locally controlled technology, such as tools that run on local networks or offline and let people share information and report violence without relying on large platforms. Participants named cost, usability and signal as obstacles for such tools, and noted that earlier open-source options have been abandoned. They added that any AI tools built for survivors should guarantee privacy, referral to a human and an emergency pathway.

Participants from the creative sector described several personal guardrails, such as keeping their own writing in a closed project folder and not using general chat tools for work they intend to publish. The report also states that the burden of literacy should not fall on users alone, and that many people feel too disempowered to set limits. Artists who took part said that once a work is in a training pool, it cannot be removed. Our inference is that such practices protect only future work, and do not reach content that has already been scraped.

South Korea's Framework Act on the Development of Artificial Intelligence and the Creation of a Foundation for Trust, which the Ministry of Science and ICT says took full effect on 22 January 2026, sets out obligations for a defined category of high-impact AI, meaning systems used in listed areas that may significantly affect people's life, physical safety or fundamental rights, whereas the July version of the Philippine substitute bill described above requires registration only for high-risk systems. Businesses providing high-impact AI must put in place risk management, explanation and user protection measures, human oversight and documentation. On disclosure, Article 31(1) in the Korea Legislation Research Institute's English translation of the Act (Act No. 20676) requires operators to tell users in advance that a product or service runs on high-impact or generative AI. The Ministry of Science and ICT announced that fact-finding investigations and penalties under the transparency provision will be deferred for a grace period of at least a year (both checked on 1 November).

Two provisions of Taiwan's AI Basic Act (人工智慧基本法), in force since its promulgation on 14 January 2026, are addressed to government: Article 19 requires the government to carry out risk assessments when it uses AI and to set usage rules or internal control mechanisms, and Article 14 requires the competent authorities, in consultation with the personal data protection authority, to avoid unnecessary collection, processing or use of personal data in AI research and applications. Article 4 lists transparency and explainability among the Act's principles without saying to whom disclosure is owed (Articles 4 and 19 checked on 29 October, Article 14 on 23 October). In Hong Kong, the Digital Policy Office's Artificial Intelligence Adoption Guide for Government Bureaux and Departments (July 2026), written as recommendations without stating binding force, advises that important decisions should never depend exclusively on AI outputs without human review. The guide does not require telling the people affected by a decision that AI was involved (checked on 29 October).

When comparing AI governance across places, questions on rights include which training data and data collection companies must disclose, whether the people affected can contest AI-assisted decisions, and whether oversight bodies have a legal mandate and permanence. On what the policy is meant to achieve, one can also ask whether registering only high-risk systems, as in the July version, can both leave room for startups and be enforced in practice by regulators.

item.title: Personal protection and open source maintenance as AI speeds up vulnerability discovery
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: In two posts on 23 October, EFF argued that frontier AI models have made finding vulnerabilities cheap and that computers will be compromised more often. EFF recommends that everyone keep browsers and apps updated, use a password manager and watch for phishing, and argues that companies relying on open source should contribute money and people to its upkeep. People who run their own websites should also check that PHP has been patched.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 19 sources, including EFF, The PHP Foundation, PHP

EFF, the US digital rights organisation, published two posts on 23 October arguing that frontier AI models from companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic have made it cheap and easy to find zero-day vulnerabilities (flaws the vendor does not yet know about and has not fixed). EFF expects things to get worse before they get better, and its first post offers basic digital security habits that apply to anyone using a computer or phone, wherever they are. The second post uses vulnerabilities in PHP as its example and argues that companies relying on open source should contribute money and people to its upkeep. Anyone whose website runs on PHP should also check that the PHP on the server has been patched against the vulnerabilities disclosed in October.

According to EFF's second post, the US National Vulnerability Database (NVD) holds around 400,000 CVEs (the shared identifiers for publicly disclosed vulnerabilities) filed since 1988, and 13,000 new ones were submitted in October alone. From this EFF calculates that 3% of all vulnerabilities ever logged were found in October, and says it is likely that by the end of the year more than a quarter of all vulnerabilities ever found will date from 2026. There is no primary link for these figures in the post, and the source given in the chart caption is CVE Tracker. An analysis by the security firm Brandefense, updated on 26 October, lists 86,533 CVE records published in the NVD by 25 October, against 48,151 for the whole of 2025.

EFF's second post takes PHP, a programming language widely used on web servers, as its example and says it powers nearly 70% of websites. W3Techs statistics for 2 November put the figure at 69.1% of websites whose server-side language is known. On 21 October the PHP project released 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35, fixing two vulnerabilities that allow an attacker who is not logged in to execute code on the server.

According to a 21 October post by the PHP Foundation, which funds PHP development, signs of the problem had surfaced during the first externally funded audit in 2024, but no concrete attack path was found. According to EFF, because the maintainers could not find a way to exploit it at the time, they lowered its priority and the vulnerability went unfixed. In EFF's account, researchers working with the latest models from OpenAI and Anthropic independently rediscovered it in August 2026 and found a way to exploit it. The foundation lists the security firm Calif, OpenAI and Wiz as the discoverers, and mentions Anthropic's Claude Mythos only in a section on its own scan of PHP earlier in 2026, not as a discoverer.

According to EFF, at the time of writing more than 33 million websites were still running vulnerable versions of PHP. On 27 October The New Stack cited internet-wide scans by the security firm Censys, in which about 32.5 million internet-facing PHP services reported unsafe versions and about 61.3 million could not be identified by version. According to the same article, Linux distributions often backport fixes to older versions without changing the version number. Some services counted as unpatched may therefore already be patched, and estimates based on version numbers may run high.

In EFF's description, projects such as PHP, OpenSSL and SQLite run on nearly every computer, and some are maintained by teams as small as one person. Vulnerability reports are now pouring in, some of them false but many of them real. According to the foundation, PHP's security team published 15 CVEs between 1 July and 21 October and worked through more than 100 reports that turned out to be invalid, duplicates or not reproducible. AI helps the team validate reports, but a person makes every decision and works on every patch.

Perspective

A CVE is a numbered record of a publicly disclosed vulnerability, and records vary widely in severity, yet EFF's second post calls them all critical security bugs. In June, Help Net Security reported a full-year CVE forecast from FIRST, the international association of incident response teams, and noted that part of the growth comes from GitHub Security Advisories and VulnCheck expanding their cataloguing and backfilling old records.

According to the same Brandefense analysis, there were 272 additions in 2026, up to 23 October, to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog of the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), or about three for every thousand CVEs. The analysis adds that KEV includes older CVEs, so the ratio is only a rough guide. Our inference is that the growth in CVE records does not translate into the same growth in exploited vulnerabilities, though the number of patches people need to apply has gone up.

On funding open source, EFF argues that companies should put money and people into maintaining the open source projects they depend on, without proposing amounts, mechanisms or a specific fund. The PHP Foundation's account of PHP's resources differs from EFF's: in EFF's post maintenance depends on a small number of volunteers working in their free time, while in the foundation's post security work on PHP itself depends on a small group of foundation-funded developers and a little volunteer help. The foundation asks for support from three groups, namely companies that build products with PHP, hosting providers along with cloud providers and Linux distributions, and governments and public institutions. It also acknowledges that the delayed fix was "a structural failure, caused by both the security team's decision process and its lack of resources."

EFF's first recommendation for individuals is to keep the browser and all apps up to date with the latest patches. According to EFF's Surveillance Self-Defense guide (SSD), updates often fix security problems in older code that attacks can exploit, and some older operating systems no longer receive even security updates. According to Chrome's help page, the browser updates itself in the background when a new version is available, usually completing the update when it is closed and reopened. If the browser stays open for a long time, an indicator shows that an update is waiting.

EFF also recommends installing a password manager and using a different password for each website, so that one compromised site does not expose the passwords for other accounts. According to SSD, the password managers built in by Apple, Google and Mozilla are also an option. Apple's Passwords app is end-to-end encrypted by default, while Google's password manager only gets on-device encryption if users go into the settings and set a passphrase themselves. Standalone password managers such as Bitwarden and KeePassXC are also on SSD's list, and according to the same guide, automatically filling in a password is an important protection against phishing.

EFF further suggests considering a tracker-blocking tool such as Privacy Badger, its free browser extension, available for Safari according to the 23 October post. The same sentence urges vigilance against phishing, which according to SSD means tricking people into handing over their passwords through a deceptive link. EFF also warns that data breaches may become more likely and that the websites people visit may face more attacks than usual, so some services may be disrupted.

For people who run a blog or website, EFF recommends making sure that they or their hosting provider have patched the PHP vulnerabilities. According to the php.net advisory of 21 October, there are no complete mitigations and updating is the only safe choice. The PHP project also provided minimal backports for 7.4, 8.0 and 8.1 for people who build PHP from source, while for other older versions it depends on whether a distribution or a long-term support (LTS) vendor offers a backport. From EFF's advice that site owners or their hosting provider should patch, our inference is that people on hosted plans can ask their provider to confirm that this fix has been applied.

Disruption of the kind EFF warns about appeared in Japan around the PHP release, although what we found were organisations going offline ahead of the fix rather than confirmed attacks. On the evening of 21 October, according to ITmedia NEWS, Japan's prime minister urged organisations on X to prepare to apply the fix that night, adding that temporarily taking a website offline is one way to reduce the risk where patching is difficult. The security blog piyolog, compiling organisations' notices and news reports rather than official statistics, counted 211 organisations in Japan that had suspended services or announced emergency maintenance, in a count made during the 01:00 hour, Japan time, on 22 October. These included 2 national government bodies, 4 local governments and 7 financial institutions, though some of the notices did not name PHP and some organisations were counted on the basis of news reports.

In South Korea, the Korea Internet & Security Agency (KISA) published guidance for companies on 22 October, advising those who can neither update nor apply interim settings to consider blocking external access or temporarily suspending services. Taiwan's Administration for Cyber Security, under the Ministry of Digital Affairs, issued a press release the same day asking organisations to take stock of their PHP systems, patch them and then review their system logs, without asking anyone to suspend services. As of 22 October we, a community based in Taiwan, found no notices of Taiwanese organisations going offline over these flaws, and no confirmed intrusions in Japan, South Korea or Taiwan.

The first step that applies to everyone using a computer or phone is to turn on automatic updates for the system and apps, and to close and reopen the browser from time to time. On iPhone the setting is under Settings > General > Software Update > Automatic Updates (our translation of the menu names on Apple's Taiwan support page), and according to Apple's support page updates install overnight while the phone is charging and connected to Wi-Fi. According to Android's help page, most security patches install automatically, on a schedule that varies by manufacturer and carrier, and older devices may not be able to run newer Android versions. Our inference is that these settings cannot prevent breaches caused by a website itself being compromised, while using a different password on each site keeps one breach from spreading to other accounts.

item.title: Law enforcement claims tying Pixel phones and GrapheneOS to crime, and the disputes around them
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: In September a police source in Toronto told The Globe and Mail that a key phone in a shooting investigation runs GrapheneOS, a privacy-hardened operating system that supports only Pixel phones, and that investigators had not been able to unlock it. From 31 October the GrapheneOS account posted a series of messages alleging a state-sponsored smear campaign in the Netherlands and Germany. Law enforcement in Canada, Spain and France and GrapheneOS each give their own account of who uses it, whether it can be unlocked and what developers are responsible for.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 21 sources, including GrapheneOS, The Globe and Mail, Xataka Android

GrapheneOS, a privacy-hardened operating system that supports only Google Pixel phones, has been tied to criminal investigations by law enforcement in Spain, France and Canada again and again since 2025. Between 31 October and 1 November its official account posted a series of messages on Mastodon alleging a state-sponsored misinformation and smear campaign in the Netherlands and Germany, while calling The Globe and Mail's September article fair and balanced. As of 2 November, none of the material we found included any notice asking people to change phone system settings, so our judgement is that readers who use a Pixel do not need to change anything. On the same day we also found no similar public statement from law enforcement in Asia.

According to The Globe and Mail's 21 September report, a key phone seized in connection with a series of shootings in Toronto runs GrapheneOS, and investigators had not been able to unlock it by the time of the report, which has held up the investigation. The only source for this is one police source, who is not authorized to discuss the case and whom the paper does not identify. The Toronto Police Service replied that it cannot comment on the status of a particular forensic examination, and a spokesperson added that law enforcement needs appropriate lawful tools to keep pace with encryption.

The report also says that Toronto's police chief publicly supports Bill C-22, which was before Canada's federal Parliament at the time of the 21 September report. The bill would require electronic service providers to help intercept data, and tech companies and civil liberties advocates have opposed it.

Similar claims appeared as early as July 2025. Xataka Android relayed a report by the Catalan outlet Ara in which an anti-drug official in the Catalan police said that every time they see a Pixel, they think it could be a drug trafficker. A security expert quoted in the article put this down to the fact that a Pixel lets its owner freely install another operating system.

The French version came in November 2025. According to Clubic's account of a Le Parisien report, cybersecurity analysts at France's judicial police sent an internal alert about GrapheneOS to other law enforcement services. The alert describes GrapheneOS as initially presented for legitimate uses, protecting citizens against intrusions on their phones, before gradually spreading to users who above all want to escape any collection or analysis of their devices' data by the authorities, including in judicial proceedings. According to Privacy Guides, GrapheneOS then announced it was ending its operations in France and moving its servers away from the French hosting company OVH.

Perspective

According to GrapheneOS's official FAQ, supported devices are chosen against a list of requirements. These include full hardware security functionality when running an alternate operating system, verified boot (a check at startup that the system has not been altered) and complete monthly security patches without any regular delay longer than a week. The FAQ states that the Pixel 8 through the Pixel 10a meet them, and these are requirements GrapheneOS sets for itself, not a third-party verification. The Pixel itself is an ordinary retail phone, sold on the Google Store in Taiwan, Japan and Singapore among other places.

Who uses GrapheneOS is where the accounts differ most. According to GIGAZINE's account of GrapheneOS's July 2025 response, the majority of criminals use iOS or Android, and the proportion of criminals among GrapheneOS users may be even lower than on Android. In the material we found, no party has published statistics on who makes up the user base. An EFF technologist interviewed by The Globe and Mail said there are many reasons to choose GrapheneOS, and that they have nothing to do with whether someone is committing crimes.

Accounts of whether the phones can be unlocked do not agree either. GrapheneOS's statement to The Globe and Mail, sent through its lawyer, says the system is designed so that the project itself cannot bypass its security protections, and that there are no backdoors, master keys or remote access capabilities. The report interviewed a retired Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) officer who runs a digital forensics firm, and speaking about phones in general, he said the tools from Cellebrite and Magnet Forensics, two makers of phone forensics tools, can unlock pretty much any phone. Neither company would comment on whether it has ever extracted data from a phone running GrapheneOS, and the RCMP and the FBI also declined to comment.

According to Xataka Android, when the Catalan police cannot break the encryption, they infect suspects' phones with malware under court authorization. The article quotes one line, without naming who said it: against organized crime, "si no metes troyanos, estás muerto" (without trojans, you get nowhere). Some lawyers question the tactic, saying the limits on how far it intrudes on privacy are unclear.

On developers' responsibility, according to Privacy Guides' account of a Le Parisien interview, France's cybercrime prosecutor said that a certain portion of users have a real legitimate interest in protecting their communications. If links to a criminal organization are found and the developers do not cooperate with the law, prosecutors will still take them to court. A GrapheneOS social media post quoted by The Globe and Mail says that GrapheneOS is completely legal and that the project has no obligation to weaken any of its security protections. A University of Toronto professor interviewed in the report said there is no legal prohibition in Canada on using a privacy-focused operating system, and that in some cases it may be essential for political dissidents, activists and journalists.

GrapheneOS's 31 October post said that Murena, the company that develops /e/OS, another de-Googled phone operating system, is directly assisting state anti-privacy campaigns and has repeatedly claimed that GrapheneOS is mainly used by criminals. This is GrapheneOS's claim, and we found nothing else to corroborate it.

One of the examples the post links to is a March 2026 Clubic interview with Murena's founder, in which the passage comes from his answer to a question about whether supporting many phone models comes at the cost of security. He said /e/OS lets its users escape the mass collection of personal data on phones on the market, not help child sex offenders slip under the radar of justice. In the same answer he went on to say that /e/OS is not a system aimed at hardened security that would be useful only to targeted people.

As of 2 November we had found no response from Murena to these posts, and no statement from Google about Pixel phones being linked to crime. A GrapheneOS post on 1 November also said that Dutch law enforcement has spent years overstating its own capabilities and making GrapheneOS's security out to be weaker than it is. We have no verifiable primary source for what law enforcement in the Netherlands and Germany actually said, and what this article says about both countries comes only from GrapheneOS's posts.

None of the material we found includes any notice asking people to change phone system settings, and our judgement is that readers using a Pixel's stock system or already running GrapheneOS do not need to change their settings because of these disputes. According to the official FAQ, some companies sell phones with GrapheneOS preinstalled, and as of 2 November the project was not affiliated with or endorsing any of them. The project recommends buying a supported Pixel and installing it yourself (the web installer needs only a browser with WebUSB support, meaning one that lets a web page connect to the phone over USB), and GrapheneOS's 1 November post also says that companies in the Netherlands sell counterfeit GrapheneOS devices. Our inference is that installing it yourself avoids a tampered system, but does nothing to change how local laws treat seized phones and demands to hand over passwords.

As of 2 November we had not found any public statement from police in mainland China, Hong Kong, Singapore or Taiwan tying encrypted phones or a particular operating system, GrapheneOS included, to crime. Installing GrapheneOS yourself also depends on reaching the project's servers, and according to the installer's code it downloads from releases.grapheneos.org, which the third-party monitor GreatFire found disrupted in mainland China in its last test on 2 October, with only one conclusive test in the preceding 90 days. Mainland China, Hong Kong, Singapore and Taiwan do have rules on what happens after a phone is seized, which apply to any device and are not statements by law enforcement about a particular system. Amended implementation rules gazetted in Hong Kong on 23 March 2026 let police investigating offences endangering national security require a "specified person" to provide the password or decryption method for an electronic device, and failing to comply without reasonable excuse carries a fine of up to HK$100,000 and one year in prison.

Under section 40 of Singapore's Criminal Procedure Code 2010, an officer authorized by order of the Public Prosecutor can require a person to hand over decryption information when investigating an arrestable offence, with a penalty of up to S$10,000, three years in prison, or both. A draft rule on electronic evidence released for public comment by mainland China's Ministry of Public Security on 22 May 2026 lets police, when the holder will not provide account passwords, take measures to obtain them with the approval of a public security official at county level or above. Where not extracting the data immediately could lead to serious consequences such as its loss, the draft lets police obtain the passwords first and complete the approval within 24 hours, and as of 7 October we had found no final version. Taiwan's Code of Criminal Procedure gives the accused the right to remain silent (Article 95) and lets an order be made for the owner or holder of an item subject to seizure to produce it (Article 133), but neither article mentions passwords.

Things to watch next are the progress of Bill C-22 and whether Murena and Google respond. The bill was still before the Canadian Parliament at the time of the 21 September report, and we have not checked its progress since.

When comparing what law enforcement says in different places, on the investigative side it is worth asking whether singling out a phone or an operating system helps solve cases, and whether court-authorized measures are already enough. On the privacy side, it is worth asking whether such claims push ordinary users toward phones with weaker protection, and whether requiring developers to assist would weaken protection for every user.
