item.title: Measurements of censorship and code security gaps in China's open-weight Qwen models
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: In October, two companies that publish modified versions of Qwen models each released their own measurements, one of censorship in answers to political questions in Chinese, the other of a gap in code security that follows the client named in the prompt. The findings concern people who ask Qwen political questions and developers who write code with Qwen3-Coder, whether the model runs locally or through a service. As of 1 November, we had found no third-party replication and no response from the Qwen team.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 16 sources, including Interpretic AI, Hirundo, PNAS Nexus

Two companies published measurements of Alibaba's Qwen family of open-weight models in late October (open-weight models are models whose files are public and can be downloaded and run on your own computer). Interpretic AI measured how often Qwen3.8-27B censors its answers to political questions in Chinese, and on 31 October released a version with the censorship removed on Hugging Face. According to measurements Hirundo published on its blog on 21 October, the security of the code Qwen3-Coder writes changes with the client named in the system prompt (the instructions a developer gives the model in advance), and the company has also released a modified version.

Both studies come from companies that publish the modified models, and Hirundo also evaluates and fixes models for organisations that run open-weight models. As of 1 November we had found no third-party replication, so all the figures below are each company's own measurements. Interpretic's measurements matter to people who ask Qwen political questions, and Hirundo's to developers who write code with Qwen3-Coder.

According to Interpretic's model page, the test put to the model, in Chinese, a set of 145 political questions that two researchers published in the journal PNAS Nexus, and another language model judged whether each answer was censored. Of the 113 politically sensitive questions in the set, 98 answers from the original Qwen3.8-27B were judged censored (86.7%), against 4 (3.5%) for the modified version. The model page does not say which model did the grading or whether anyone checked samples by hand, and it describes the removal only as a "targeted weight edit", with no paper or code. Interpretic lists as limitations that the political questions were tested only in Chinese, and cautions that a substantive answer is not necessarily a correct one.

The question set comes from a paper published in February 2026, in which the researchers compared foundation models developed in China with those developed elsewhere. According to the abstract, models developed in China refused more of the 145 political questions, gave shorter answers and gave more inaccurate ones. Every model refused more often when asked in Chinese than in English, but the gap between languages was smaller than the gap between Chinese and non-Chinese models.

According to Hirundo's blog, the study asked Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct to write the same web service again and again, with user registration, login and storage of private text. Each time, only the one sentence in the system prompt saying who the code was for changed, naming a neutral client, a US defence contractor, a Chinese defence contractor or a Hong Kong pro-democracy group. The finished apps were run on BaxBench, a public benchmark from ETH Zurich and LogicStar, and an app counted as exploitable if at least one off-the-shelf attack against it succeeded.

Apps written for the US defence contractor were exploitable 70% of the time, against 59% for the Chinese defence contractor. On private data leaks, nearly half of the apps written for the Hong Kong pro-democracy group let any logged-in user read everyone's private data, against about a third for the neutral client (a relative increase of 28%, as the blog calculates it). In the group whose prompts also included security instructions, 74% of the apps for the US contractor were exploitable, against 59% for the neutral client. According to the blog's statistical tests, none of the three gaps is likely to be due to chance.

The Q&A in the blog's appendix also states that the study cannot tell whether anyone put the gap into the model on purpose. Small models write vulnerable code anyway, and about a third of the neutral client's apps leaked as well, so what the study measured is the extra risk on top of that. Only one model and one task were tested, and the task was the one with the clearest gap in a small sample of 11 tasks. The US and Hong Kong groups were deliberately chosen edge cases.

Hirundo's modified model is public on Hugging Face, and its model page describes the method as behavioral unlearning (extra training that makes a model forget a specific behaviour while keeping its other abilities). According to the blog, on CCPC-500, a 500-question benchmark Hirundo built itself, the share of answers judged to contain censorship, bias or propaganda fell from 46.6% to 4.0%, and the three code gaps were no longer significant. In other comparisons in the appendix, the modified model still showed one significant gap for the US contractor against the neutral client, and in the blog's reading the effect moves from the country to the type of organisation. On ten other programming tasks, the shares of apps that worked and of apps that were exploitable were both close to those of the original model.

Perspective

A language model's answers depend on its training data and on alignment, the later stage of training that makes a model answer according to the developer's rules. Both studies measured by asking large numbers of questions and computing proportions from the output, and neither examined training data and alignment separately. Hirundo's blog argues that the modified model's results prove the code gaps sit in the model weights, and the claim rests on the same company's own removal experiment.

SpeechMap, a public research project, tested the earlier Qwen3 generation in May 2025, and according to its roundup Qwen3's open-weight models were broadly censored on topics critical of China. The censorship was most thorough with questions asked in Chinese, present in English too, and appeared in Finnish only in some cases and less consistently. The same roundup records a high number of API errors from the commercial Qwen-Max, which SpeechMap reads as an additional layer of censorship at the API. From this we infer that when a model is used through a service, the answers may be shaped both by the model itself and by filtering on the service side.

China's Interim Measures for the Management of Generative Artificial Intelligence Services took effect on 15 August 2023, and Article 4 requires that providing and using generative AI services must not generate content inciting subversion of state power or the overthrow of the socialist system, among other categories. Under Article 2, research and application that do not provide services to the public in mainland China fall outside the Measures, and we found no provision specifically on publishing model weights. The researchers behind the PNAS Nexus paper caution that their study is observational and cross-sectional (it compares different models at a single point in time, without experiments) and "does not establish a causal linkage between regulatory pressures and censorship behaviors of China-originating LLMs".

On 3 February 2025, Taiwan's Executive Yuan required all public agencies to stop using DeepSeek AI services, and its press release noted that the security risk of data being uploaded to China had been neither clarified nor ruled out, and that the model's training involved data bias such as ideological censorship. According to the Administration for Cyber Security on 20 February 2025, the ban covered cloud services, apps and locally downloaded use, and at the time placed no restriction on use by the general public. The notices named DeepSeek, and we found none naming Qwen.

We, a community based in Taiwan, compared rules on generative AI from mainland China, Taiwan and South Korea, and neither the Taiwanese nor the South Korean rules discussed here regulate the political position of a model's answers. Besides Article 4 of the Interim Measures, mainland China has guidelines on deploying large AI models in government work, issued by the Office of the Central Cyberspace Affairs Commission and the National Development and Reform Commission and published on 10 October 2025 as a reference for government departments' own use, which call on those departments to use mature models and services that have completed filing with the cyberspace authorities for general-purpose tasks such as question answering and drafting documents (filing is a condition of entry, and the guidelines do not say what it examines). Taiwan's DeepSeek ban works on use instead, limiting which products public agencies may use. Article 31 of South Korea's Framework Act on the Development of Artificial Intelligence and the Creation of a Foundation for Trust, in full force since 22 January 2026, requires a business providing generative AI to label the output as generated by generative AI, and according to the Ministry of Science and ICT, fact-finding investigations and penalties under this transparency provision are deferred for a grace period of at least one year (checked on 1 November).

In Interpretic's tests, the modified model refused 95 of 100 harmful requests, down from 100, and its scores on general ability tests dropped slightly, side effects that anyone thinking of switching to it has to weigh. Both companies' modified models keep the original's Apache 2.0 licence, but Interpretic published no paper or code, and Hirundo described only the category of its method. Hirundo's blog states that it intends to release CCPC-500, but when we checked on 1 November the dataset's address could not be accessed (it returned a 401 error), so we cannot confirm that it is public. According to SpeechMap's roundup of May 2025, third-party modifications of the Chinese open-source models of the time had brought clear improvements in English and only modest ones in Chinese.

For people who use Qwen to look up sensitive subjects such as politics or history, we suggest putting the same question to models from different sources, then checking the answers against news coverage and primary materials. According to both the paper's abstract and SpeechMap, asking in Chinese produced more refusals or censorship, and from this we infer that asking again in another language may produce a different answer, though the paper also notes that the language gap is smaller than the gap between Chinese and non-Chinese models. None of these studies evaluated whether such approaches recover censored content, and questions that were not tested are not necessarily free of bias (our inference).

Developers writing code with Qwen3-Coder or any other model still need to review and test it separately before it goes into production. According to Hirundo's blog, adding security instructions to the prompt did not remove the gap, and common static analysis tools may not catch this kind of leak, where a logged-in user can read other people's data. On the ten other tasks, about a quarter of the apps written by the modified model were still exploitable, and the neutral client's apps leaked too (see above). From this we infer that, whichever version you use, access control checks are a good place to start a review.

As of 1 November, we had found no public response from Alibaba or the Qwen team to either study or to the paper. In early December, it will be worth watching whether any third party replicates the two companies' measurements, whether CCPC-500 is published, and whether the Qwen team responds.

item.title: The ad exception for Gmail and Photos data in Google's privacy policy
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: The 16 October version of Google's privacy policy adds an exception to its rule against personalized ads based on Drive, Gmail and Photos content, for users who choose to make that data available to other Google services that support personalized ads, such as through Personal Intelligence. People who have not connected these apps need not change anything, and as of 1 November those who have can review or disconnect them under Search Services Personalization in their Google Account.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 16 sources, including Google, The Verge, Ars Technica

The version of Google's privacy policy that took effect on 16 October adds an exception to the sentence saying Google does not show personalized ads based on content from Drive, Gmail or Photos. The exception applies when users choose to make data from these services available to other Google services that support personalized ads, and people who have not made that choice are outside it. The example given in the policy's additional context is Personal Intelligence, which, according to a Google Search help page, people aged 18 or over who are signed in to a personal Google Account can turn on themselves. As of 1 November, the supported countries and territories on that page included Taiwan, Hong Kong, Macau, Japan, South Korea and Singapore, and connecting Google Photos is not available in every region.

According to The Verge's report of 23 October, people who have already used Personal Intelligence to connect Gmail or Photos to AI Mode (a search feature that answers questions conversationally) and other Search tools may now see ads based on the content of their email and photos. Google's comparison of the two versions shows that the 1 October text did not have the closing clause "unless you choose to make data from these services available to other Google services that support personalized ads". A new sentence states that users may allow Search or Gemini Apps to access data from Photos, Gmail and Drive, and that Search may process some of that data to personalize content, including ads. The sentence on ads also changed from ads based on "interests and activity" to ads based on "interests, activity, or personalized content from Google services".

In the example in the policy's additional context, a user asks Search about a recent hotel booking, and Search may use booking details from an email to suggest things to do near the hotel. According to the Search help page, connecting once gives all Search services access to Gmail and Photos, including Google Search, AI Mode, Discover (the feed of recommended articles on the Google app's home screen), Maps, Shopping, Flights, Hotels, Translate and News. Drive, which the policy mentions, was not among the apps that could be connected on the help page when we checked on 1 November. Ask Maps in Google Maps (a feature for asking about routes and places conversationally) can also be connected to Gmail, and as of 1 November its listed regions in Asia were only India, Japan and Indonesia, not Taiwan.

Perspective

The first sentence of Google's full statement, published by Ars Technica on 23 October, is that connecting apps is entirely opt-in. The statement goes on to say that ads will continue to be relevant to things like the query, the context of the response and the user's interests, and will not be based directly on the Gmail inbox or Photos library. According to the Q&A on the Search help page, advertisers do not get access to the inbox or Photos, and Google does not show personalized ads based on sensitive categories such as race, religion, sexual orientation or health. As of 1 November, we found statements only from Google and the press, with no public response from advocacy groups or data protection authorities.

The help page's answer on ads likewise says ads will not be based directly on the inbox or Photos library, then adds that Search may reference summaries, excerpts and inferences from these sources to personalize the experience, and that "That same info may be used to show you ads". Read this way, ads are not based on the inbox or library themselves, while the summaries, excerpts and inferences Search derives from email and photos may be used for ads. The same page's answer on training AI models includes an example of how Search pulls email and photos together. When a user asks AI Mode to suggest restaurants for an upcoming trip, the models might look at emails and photos for the hotel reservation and flight itinerary, then summarize that information into recommendations.

According to the help page, Search services do not train generative AI models directly on the Gmail inbox or on imagery and audio from the Photos library. The page goes on to state that when users interact with Search, summaries, excerpts and inferences from relevant emails, files and media are used to train the models. Where an email is brief or particularly relevant to the question, the summary may be the email itself. Once apps are connected, a subset of the data processed by AI Mode and Ask Maps is reviewed by human reviewers, including trained service providers.

We, a community based in Taiwan, looked at how the feature is offered in Asia, which The Verge's report does not cover. As of 1 November, the Search help page's supported countries and territories for connecting content apps included, among others, Hong Kong, Japan, Macau, Malaysia, Singapore, South Korea and Taiwan, with Chinese (Traditional), Chinese (Simplified), Japanese and Korean among the languages, and mainland China was not on the list. For the Gemini version, GIGAZINE reported that Google Japan posted on X on 14 April 2026 that Personal Intelligence in Gemini had begun a phased rollout in Japan, to be completed within a week. For Hong Kong, South Korea, Singapore and Taiwan we found no official launch announcement for the Gemini version, and the Gemini help page gives no country list.

None of the following provisions or policy plans is aimed at features that connect email or photos to ads, and we did not check how any of them would apply here, but they point in different directions. Taiwan and mainland China work through refusal, with Article 20 of Taiwan's Personal Data Protection Act requiring a non-government entity that markets with personal data to stop once the person objects and to offer a way to object the first time, and Article 24 of mainland China's Personal Information Protection Law requiring marketing through automated decision-making to come with an option that does not target personal characteristics or a convenient way to refuse. Under a policy plan South Korea's Personal Information Protection Commission published on 31 January 2024, by contrast, advertisers that do not identify a specific person may process online behavioural data without consent, provided that accumulating, overlapping or combining the data does not make anyone identifiable, while identifying a person requires consent. We could not find whether the revised guidelines the Commission planned to issue by the end of 2024 are in force, and readers can ask whether a way to refuse, an option not to be targeted or a consent requirement tied to identification reaches ads shaped by summaries and inferences from data a user connected for a different feature.

People who have not connected Gmail or Photos to Search or Gemini do not need to change any settings. Those who have can follow the Search help page: on a computer, go to Search Services Personalization in the Google Account, then Additional Personal Intelligence > Connected Content Apps, to review or disconnect them. Anyone who wants to try the feature first turns on Personalized Recommendations in the same place and then connects, and the actual screens may differ from the instructions (as of 1 November, a banner at the top of the help page said the settings are being updated). In Gemini the connections are under Settings & help > Personal Intelligence > Connected Apps at the bottom of gemini.google.com, and the service named in the policy as processing this data to personalize content, including ads, is Search, with no mention of Gemini.

The connection settings in Search cover whether Gmail and Photos data is made available to Search, and My Ad Center is a separate set of controls. Under the policy, the ad settings in My Ad Center control what information Google uses to show ads, but the My Ad Center help page does not say whether its personalized ads switch covers connected data. Besides connecting the apps, the Search help page requires turning on Smart features in other Google products in Gmail as a condition for personalized responses. According to the Gmail help page, this setting controls the use of Workspace data in other Google products, and the page does not mention Photos or ads.

Going by the example in the policy's additional context (our inference), features such as suggesting plans from hotel booking details in an email work only once the apps are connected, and disconnecting removes them. According to the Search help page, data already saved in Search Services History is not deleted when an app is disconnected and can still be used for product improvement, including training generative AI models.

item.title: Weekly brief, 2026 week 44
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: Seven stories from 13 to 23 October: Hong Kong's tighter rules on access to land records, the face search engine PimEyes and the EU AI Act's ban, Senate committee review of Canada's Bill C-22, the finding that microtargeted ads by four German parties were unlawful, a generative AI pilot for checks at France's public employment service, European governments' Palantir contracts, and the enforcement of Ofcom's fines against websites outside the UK.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 16 sources, including Hong Kong Free Press, Development Bureau, South China Morning Post

This issue collects seven stories, one of them a follow-up to an earlier article, covering 13 to 23 October.

Rules on access to land records in Hong Kong

According to a Development Bureau announcement on 16 October, the Hong Kong government gazetted eight pieces of subsidiary legislation that day. The provisions on electronic applications take effect on 4 October 2027, and the Secretary for Development will set the commencement date for the rest in the first half of 2027.

Hong Kong Free Press reported on 21 October that the new rules limit land record searches to nine purposes, and news reporting is not among them. "Public interest" is listed as a valid ground, but the Land Registrar vets every application case by case. The Hong Kong Journalists Association called for the amendments to be shelved, arguing that protecting "privacy" should not override the public's right to know, and listed 18 investigative reports produced using land records.

According to a Development Bureau paper to the Legislative Council quoted by Hong Kong Free Press, the purpose of the amendments is to strike a balance between protecting personal data privacy and keeping land records transparent. The South China Morning Post reported that on 23 October the Legislative Council decided to set up a subcommittee to examine them.

The face search engine PimEyes and the AI Act's ban

According to a netzpolitik.org report on 13 October, the EU's Artificial Intelligence Act has since 2 February 2025 banned AI systems that create or expand facial recognition databases through the untargeted scraping of facial images from the internet, but the face search engine PimEyes still operates as usual in Germany. The Federal Network Agency, designated as the competent authority only in summer 2026, declined to comment on planned or ongoing proceedings. A German bill would let the Federal Criminal Police Office and the Federal Police use such search engines, and according to the report, the bill's explanatory memorandum rests on the view that the ban does not apply if no AI system is used to scrape the data. As of 31 October, we had found no response from PimEyes to the report.

Senate committee review of Canada's Bill C-22

Our 20 October article, "Senate second reading of Canada's Bill C-22 and providers' responses", covered this Lawful Access Act. The bill would let the government require telecommunications and online service providers to build technical capabilities to assist law enforcement, and require designated providers to retain metadata (records about communications rather than their content). According to the bill's progress page on the Parliament of Canada website, the bill passed second reading in the Senate on 22 October and was referred to the Standing Senate Committee on National Security, Defence and Veterans Affairs. As of 31 October, the committee had no recorded activity on it.

According to the Senate Debates for the same day, the opposition critic for the bill argued that it should go to the Standing Senate Committee on Legal and Constitutional Affairs instead. The senator also noted that a House of Commons committee had amended the metadata retention period to six months. According to an Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF) article on 22 October, the Canadian Civil Liberties Association is urging people to sign a petition against the bill, and some senators have also expressed concerns.

Finding of unlawful microtargeting by four German parties

According to an announcement on 21 October by noyb, a European privacy advocacy group, the Berlin data protection authority found that the SPD, the Greens, the Left Party and the CDU targeted ads at users based on their political interests without a legal basis such as consent. dpa-AFX, part of the German Press Agency (dpa), reported that the authority made its decision on 24 September and issued only formal warnings or reprimands to the parties, with no fines. As of netzpolitik.org's report on 23 October, the penalties were not yet final, according to a spokesperson for the authority. As of 31 October, we had found no response from the four parties.

Generative AI pilot for job-search checks at France's public employment service

On 23 October, La Quadrature du Net, a French digital rights group, published a presentation that France Travail gave to its AI ethics committee on 30 June. According to the group, the public employment service is piloting generative AI to help check whether jobseekers are actively looking for work, and the group called for its immediate withdrawal.

In the presentation's own words, the AI consolidates data from the database, interviews and case files into a single report, which an adviser analyses and validates. According to the same presentation, the decision always remains with the adviser. The goals it lists are meeting the 2027 target for checks with unchanged staffing and making checks systematic by 2030.

La Quadrature du Net argues that the advisers' work will be reduced to confirming possible sanctions. As of 31 October, we had found no response from France Travail to the document.

Palantir contracts with European governments

According to a netzpolitik.org report on 15 October, an investigation led by the Dutch outlet Follow the Money, with media from 18 countries taking part, found national-level contracts with Palantir, the US data analytics software company, in 11 European countries, eight of which have dealings with the armed forces or defence ministry. According to the same report, many countries are concerned about dependence, security and democracy, and are looking for alternatives.

According to netzpolitik.org's weekly round-up, the amounts disclosed by individual countries add up to about €1.4 billion. Some governments do not disclose their costs, so this is a lower bound. In its response to the investigative team, Palantir stated that technological sovereignty should be judged by who controls the data and decisions, not only by the nationality of the software vendor.

Enforcement of Ofcom's fines against websites outside the UK

Ofcom, the UK communications regulator, has fined the forum 4chan hundreds of thousands of pounds under the Online Safety Act, and according to a report by the entertainment outlet Dexerto on 20 October, 4chan had not paid. According to the same report, Ofcom's chief executive told a House of Commons committee that some fines may never be recovered if foreign courts get in the way. The chief executive also said that only 2 of the 11 fines issued under the Act since March 2025 had been paid.

A lawyer representing 4chan described this testimony on the lawyer's own website as Ofcom conceding defeat, while Dexerto wrote that the chief executive did not name 4chan and that Ofcom has not publicly said it is abandoning enforcement. According to news from the University of Oxford's Faculty of Law, the lawsuit 4chan brought against Ofcom in the US was dismissed by a federal district court in mid-September on grounds of foreign sovereign immunity. As of 31 October, we had found no response from Ofcom or any new enforcement action.

item.title: Dispute over the removal of the Bluetooth mesh messaging app Bitchat in India
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: Bitchat, an open-source messaging app that sends messages over a Bluetooth mesh network without the internet, was removed from the App Store in India on 3 October at the request of India's Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology. As of 31 October, neither the order nor its reasons had been published, and on 11 November the Kerala High Court will hear a public interest petition seeking to suspend the block. Readers outside India are not affected by this removal.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 17 sources, including TechCrunch, SFLC.in, Internet Freedom Foundation

Bitchat, an open-source messaging app that sends messages over a Bluetooth mesh network (phones relay messages to one another without going through the internet), was removed from the App Store in India on 3 October. According to the Apple notice the developer made public, the removal followed a demand from India's Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, and no illegal content was identified in it. When TechCrunch checked that day, Bitchat could not be found on Google Play in India either, and Apple, Google and MeitY did not respond to requests for comment. The removal applies only in India, and as of 31 October the App Store lookup interface still returned Bitchat for Taiwan and Hong Kong, though not for mainland China, where it was removed separately in February (see Perspective).

Under Section 69A, the central government may, in the interest of sovereignty, defence, state security, public order and similar grounds, direct intermediaries by an order with reasons recorded in writing to block public access to information. Under the 2009 Information Technology (Procedure and Safeguards for Blocking for Access of Information by Public) Rules, the designated officer is to make all reasonable efforts to notify the person or intermediary hosting the information to appear before a committee chaired by the designated officer, with representatives of the law, home affairs and other ministries. In an emergency, the ministry's secretary may issue directions without a hearing, and the designated officer must bring the request before the committee within 48 hours. Under the same rules, all blocking requests and actions taken must be kept confidential.

As of 31 October, we, a community based in Taiwan, had found no public explanation from the government for the October removal, and two Indian digital rights groups, SFLC.in and the Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF), both wrote in statements in early October that the order and its reasons could not be found. Bitchat's developer has only posted Apple's notice on X, and we found no formal response or legal action. In its notice, Apple asks the developer to contact MeitY directly.

The government reasons we did find come from a different notice in July. On 23 July, the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre of the Ministry of Home Affairs, relying on a different provision, asked GitHub to remove Bitchat's code repositories, on the grounds that apps of this kind need no registration or phone number verification and that their architecture impedes lawful interception and law enforcement investigations. According to the same notice, such tools could be used to coordinate unlawful activity during internet shutdowns or public order incidents. According to IFF and the Indian tech policy outlet MediaNama, the July notices were reportedly withdrawn or not enforced after they became public.

Perspective

Bitchat lets nearby phones relay messages directly, up to 7 hops, with no account or phone number. When a connection is available, messages can also travel through relays on Nostr (an open, decentralised messaging protocol). According to the developer's documentation, private messages are encrypted with the Noise protocol (a framework for setting up encrypted sessions). Live sessions have forward secrecy (a key leaked later cannot decrypt earlier messages), while messages stored for offline delivery do not.

According to the developer's privacy assessment, public channel content is visible to everyone taking part. Device identifiers do not rotate, so people nearby can recognise the same device across time and places, and can tell that someone is using the app.

Bitchat is maintained by volunteers, and the iOS version is released into the public domain (anyone may freely use and modify the code). Soon after its launch in July 2025, a researcher pointed out that its identity verification was open to a man-in-the-middle attack (a third party impersonating one side of a conversation), and the security firm Trail of Bits wrote in a commentary that it should not be relied on for sensitive messages at the time. The developer then moved to Noise encryption, and according to a fix merged in June 2026, one audit found ten critical or high-risk issues. The auditor is not named in the fix, and as of 31 October we had found no complete audit report from an independent organisation.

According to SFLC.in's statement, the block appears to have no end date, and using Section 69A to block an entire messaging app is disproportionate. IFF's position is that the block is unconstitutional: Section 69A permits blocking unlawful information, and a messaging tool that works during internet shutdowns falls outside that. In the Telegram case in June, the Delhi High Court held that Section 69A can be used to block an entire app, and according to the committee opinion quoted in that judgment, that block was temporary and limited in duration.

SFLC.in notes in its statement that the removal came right after an internet shutdown on 2 October, and infers that the app may have been targeted because it allows communication during shutdowns. IFF's view is that the government objects to what the app can do, not to the content it carries. The government's reasoning in the July notice is that the architecture of such apps impedes lawful interception, and that because they keep working during shutdowns and network restrictions, they could be used to get around those restrictions.

Blocking requests are to be kept confidential under the 2009 rules, yet Apple passed the notice on to the developer. IFF is asking the government to publish the order and its reasons, and Apple to disclose the demand in its transparency report, and says it will seek a copy of the order under the Right to Information Act (the law that lets people request information from public authorities). On 14 October, the Kerala High Court heard a public interest litigation (a case brought in the public interest) and, without yet deciding whether it is maintainable, directed all respondents to file affidavits first, with the next hearing on 11 November. The respondents include government ministries and the Indian subsidiaries of Apple and Google.

According to IFF's statement, the removal does not delete the app from phones where it is already installed, but new users cannot download it and existing users stop receiving security updates. Anyone considering Bitchat can start with the white paper and privacy assessment the developer publishes on GitHub. According to these documents, public channel content is visible to everyone taking part, people nearby can detect a device running the app, and security fixes ship only in the latest version.

The iOS version requires iOS 16 or later and the Android version requires Android 8.0 or later, and both offer Traditional and Simplified Chinese interfaces. For people who care about being recognised by those nearby, this risk remains after they start using the app, and the developer lists rotating identifiers as future work.

In February 2026, the Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC) also asked Apple to remove Bitchat from the App Store in mainland China. According to the notice the developer made public in April, summarised by the Japanese tech outlet GIGAZINE, Apple named the provision relied on: Article 3 of the Provisions on the Security Assessment of Internet-based Information Services with Attribute of Public Opinions or Capable of Social Mobilization. As of 31 October, the App Store lookup interface returned no result for Bitchat in mainland China.

Under Article 3, providers of services with public opinion attributes or social mobilisation capability must carry out their own security assessments when, for example, they launch such a service, add such features or see users grow significantly, and removal is not mentioned in the article itself. Under the same provisions, a provider that has not done an assessment is first notified to do one, and one that refuses faces a public risk warning and inspection, and any violations found are to be dealt with according to law. The provisions themselves do not mention an appeal or a court, and we did not check general administrative review or judicial review. We found no published order and no end date.

According to media reports, Taiwan's Ministry of the Interior publicly announced action against Xiaohongshu (RedNote) in December 2025, requiring network access providers under the Fraud Crime Hazard Prevention Act to stop resolving its domains (so that addresses no longer lead to its servers) and restrict access, for a provisional period of one year. Unlike India's case, where neither the order nor its reasons are public, the government announced this action and cited the law. It was directed at network access providers, and app stores are not mentioned in the reports. We checked only that act and the Copyright Act, which often comes up in discussions of website blocking and in its current form contains no provision for ordering blocks, and found no provision empowering the government to order an app store to remove a particular app.

In Hong Kong, we also found no provision that specifically empowers the government to order an app store to remove a particular app. Under Schedule 4 of the Implementation Rules for Article 43 of the Law of the People's Republic of China on Safeguarding National Security in the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (as published in 2020; we have not checked later amendments), a designated officer authorised by the Commissioner of Police with the approval of the Secretary for Security may require a platform service provider to take a disabling action on an electronic message likely to constitute an offence endangering national security, without first going to a court. Schedule 4 is about electronic messages on electronic platforms, app stores are not mentioned in it, and we have not checked whether its "platform service provider" includes them.

Under Schedule 4, requirements must be in writing. A service provider charged with failing to comply has a defence if compliance could not reasonably be expected because the necessary technology was not reasonably available, or because of a risk of substantial loss to, or substantial prejudice to the rights of, a third party. Schedule 4 itself has no provision on giving reasons or a route of appeal, and we did not check general judicial review.

For both the Indian and the mainland Chinese removals, we found no published order and no end date, and Apple named only the legal basis in its notices. India's rules require the designated officer to make all reasonable efforts to notify the host or intermediary to appear before a committee, though in an emergency directions can be issued without a hearing, and a public interest petition against this removal has been filed, with the court yet to decide whether it is maintainable. In mainland China, Article 12 of the assessment provisions does provide for prior notice, but the notice asks the provider to carry out an assessment, rather than giving the developer a chance to be heard before removal. Taiwan's action against Xiaohongshu was announced publicly with the law and a one-year term, but it targeted network access rather than an app store.

When comparing approaches, it helps to ask whether a removal order is published, whether it gives reasons and an end date, and whether developers and users have a chance to be heard before removal or to seek a remedy afterwards. The intended effect of the policy belongs in the comparison too. Removal does not delete installed copies of the app, and we could find no public assessment of whether the block achieves the law enforcement aims the government has stated.

item.title: Norway's fine on Xandr over Grindr user data in real-time bidding
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: On 12 October, Norway's data protection authority announced a fine of NOK 92 million (about €8.5 million) on Xandr, an advertising technology company owned by Microsoft, for processing data on Grindr users in Norway through real-time bidding from 2018 to 2020 without a legal basis. A Microsoft spokesperson told the press the conduct predates the acquisition and the company is reviewing the decision. Users can delete the advertising ID or refuse tracking in phone settings, and the official help pages do not say whether those settings cover the other data named in the decision.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 21 sources, including Datatilsynet, noyb, netzpolitik.org

The Norwegian Data Protection Authority (Datatilsynet) announced on 12 October a fine of NOK 92 million (about €8.5 million according to the decision) on Xandr, an advertising technology company owned by Microsoft, the highest fine the authority had issued at the time of the announcement. According to the decision of 2 October, Xandr had no legal basis when it processed data on Grindr users in Norway through real-time bidding from July 2018 to April 2020, and the data included at least the fact that a person used Grindr, the advertising ID (an identifier the phone's operating system assigns to each device for advertising) and the IP address. The fine covers only users in Norway, and the decision contains no assessment of current practice. According to an explainer the authority published on 16 October, every time someone opens an app with ads, this kind of auction may be triggered.

Real-time bidding (RTB) is the mechanism by which an app or website with ad space sends user data to advertising platforms so that advertisers can bid for it within a fraction of a second. According to the decision, when a user opened Grindr, the ad request went to Xandr either directly or through MoPub, an ad mediation service. Xandr ran platforms on both the seller and buyer sides at the time, and according to the authority's press release the data could be passed on to thousands of companies.

In its decision, the authority held that using Grindr is itself information that indicates sexual orientation, which makes it special category personal data under the EU's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR, which also applies in the European Economic Area that Norway belongs to). Processing such data is prohibited in principle, and explicit consent is one of the exceptions. According to the authority's press release, Xandr's defence was that it thought Grindr had obtained users' consent. The authority concluded that the consent Grindr collected was invalid, and that Xandr, as a joint controller (one of the companies jointly deciding how data is processed), had to verify for itself that consent was valid and could not pass the responsibility on to others.

The case grew out of complaints the Norwegian Consumer Council and noyb, a European privacy advocacy group, filed in 2020 against Grindr and several adtech companies. Grindr itself was fined NOK 65 million in December 2021, a fine upheld in turn by the Privacy Appeals Board, the Oslo District Court and the Court of Appeal. According to the authority's annual report for 2025, the Court of Appeal's judgment of October 2025 was not appealed further and is final.

Perspective

A Microsoft spokesperson told netzpolitik.org, a German digital policy outlet, that the investigation and decision concern conduct before Microsoft acquired Xandr, and that the interpretation of legal standards and practice has developed since. The spokesperson added that the company is reviewing the decision and evaluating its options.

According to the decision, Xandr argued that when the investigation began, neither it nor any company in the same position could have foreseen the standards and conclusions the authority applied. The authority took this to mean industry practice, and citing the Court of Appeal, held that industry practice cannot count as a mitigating factor.

The fine was calculated on Xandr's own annual turnover. Relying on case law of the Court of Justice of the EU, the authority found that because Xandr was not part of Microsoft during the period of the infringement, using Microsoft's turnover would be neither appropriate nor necessary.

Xandr objected to basing the fine on revenue for the 2025 fiscal year, because the authority took more than a year after its advance notification (the notice before a decision) to issue the decision. The authority still used that year's revenue, but counted the long handling time as a mitigating factor and reduced the fine. Xandr also argued that the delay had harmed its ability to defend itself, which the authority did not accept.

The deadline to appeal is three weeks from receipt of the decision, and the date of receipt has not been made public. As of 31 October, the authority's English news page had no follow-up announcement.

On 12 October, noyb linked the fine to the EU's Digital Omnibus (a proposal the European Commission put forward in November 2025 to simplify digital rules), arguing that industry lobbying aims to take identifiers used for online tracking out of the GDPR. The European consumer organisation BEUC, for its part, is concerned that loosening the definition of personal data would leave the kind of consent practice found unlawful in this case without constraint.

According to the Council of the EU's press release of 21 October, the position agreed by member states keeps the existing definition of personal data and adds new provisions on pseudonymisation (replacing fields that directly identify a person with codes).

The same press release states that the new provisions aim to make it clearer to organisations how to comply. In noyb's reading of 23 October, the new pseudonymisation provisions would drastically narrow what counts as personal data.

On Android, the advertising ID can be deleted under Settings > Privacy > Ads, and on an iPhone, Settings > Privacy & Security > Tracking lets you turn off "Allow Apps to Request to Track", or turn tracking off app by app. Under Apple's rules for apps, once a user asks an app not to track, the app may not track the user with other information that identifies the user or the device either. According to Google's help page, apps may have their own settings using other types of identifiers. Neither company's page says whether the IP address and which app is in use are still sent with ad requests, so we cannot confirm whether these settings cover the other data named in the decision.

The decision contains no information about users or current practice in Asia. We, a community based in Taiwan, compared Taiwan, Japan and mainland China on two points from the case: whether using an app counts as sensitive data, and whether each company along the ad chain has to deal with consent itself. We did not check how regulators or courts in these places interpret the use of a particular app.

Article 6 of Taiwan's Personal Data Protection Act lists data on sex life, together with medical records, genetic data and criminal records, as data that in principle may not be collected, processed or used, with written consent as one of the exceptions, subject to limits: such consent does not count where the use goes beyond what the specific purpose requires or is against the person's will. The article does not mention sexual orientation. We did not check whether every company along an ad chain has to deal with consent itself under the Act, which has no provision specifically on advertising identifiers or real-time bidding.

Under Article 20 of Japan's Act on the Protection of Personal Information, acquiring "special care-required personal information" requires the person's prior consent outside the listed exceptions. The categories in the Act and its Cabinet Order include race, creed, social status, medical history and criminal record, and neither they nor the general guidelines of the Personal Information Protection Commission list sexual orientation.

The Commission's guidelines give browsing histories collected through cookies and other device identifiers, and records of the services a person uses, as examples of "personally referable information". Under Article 31, when the recipient is expected to acquire such information as personal data identifying the person, the company providing it has to confirm beforehand that the person's consent has been obtained. According to section 3-7-2-2 of the guidelines, the consent is to be obtained by the recipient, which deals with the person and uses the information, though the provider may obtain it on the recipient's behalf, provided the person's rights are equally protected.

In Norway the company receiving the data was held responsible for checking the consent collected upstream, while for personally referable information under Article 31 the check sits with the company providing it (our comparison). A company acquiring special care-required personal information has to obtain the person's prior consent itself under Article 20(2). Article 30(1) separately requires a company receiving personal data from a third party to confirm the provider's name and address and how the provider acquired the data, unless an exception in Article 27(1) or (5) applies.

Article 28 of mainland China's Personal Information Protection Law lists biometrics, religious belief, specific identity, medical health, financial accounts, whereabouts and similar information as sensitive personal information, without mentioning sexual orientation, and under Article 29 handling sensitive personal information requires the person's separate consent. A January 2026 Q&A by the Cyberspace Administration of China, citing the national standard GB/T 45574-2025, lists common categories of sensitive personal information without sexual orientation, and we did not read the standard itself.

The Norwegian conclusion concerned Xandr's responsibility as a joint controller, which corresponds to Article 20 of the Chinese law (our comparison). Handlers that jointly decide the purpose and method of processing must agree on their respective rights and duties, and under Article 20(2) they are jointly and severally liable for harm to rights and interests in personal information. Providing personal information to another handler is a different relationship covered by Article 23, under which the provider itself has to tell the person who the recipient is, its purpose and the types of information and obtain separate consent, while the recipient has to stay within that purpose, method and scope or obtain consent again. Unlike Japan's Article 31, where the provider confirms that consent has been obtained, Article 23 has the provider obtain the consent (our comparison), and we did not check whether passing data along an ad chain counts as joint processing or as provision under Chinese law.

Comparing approaches across places, readers can ask whether using an app is treated as sensitive data, and whether every company along the ad chain that receives the data has to verify consent itself. Another question is how regulators assess past practice when a company argues that the interpretation of legal standards has since developed. If other places follow the Digital Omnibus in adjusting the definition of personal data, whether identifiers used for tracking remain covered is also worth comparing. The intended effect of the policy matters too: this case went from complaint in 2020 to decision in 2026, and the question is whether the fine can change what companies do now.

item.title: Content takedown disputes in Indonesia and a civil society coalition weighing legal action
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: In October, the Indonesian digital rights group SAFEnet reviewed two years of digital controls under the current government and recorded at least 73 pieces of content taken down between April and September 2026, most of them critical of the government. SAFEnet and other groups are also gathering potential plaintiffs to assess legal action against the Ministry of Communication and Digital Affairs. The ministry denies asking platforms to restrict content about forest fires, and in September the Constitutional Court ruled that the government must give notice with reasons before cutting off access. Readers outside Indonesia are not directly affected.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 18 sources, including SAFEnet, Pasal.id, Bisnis.com

On 21 October, the Indonesian digital rights group SAFEnet published a report on two years of digital controls under the current president and vice president, arguing that digital space is increasingly becoming a site of repression, surveillance and censorship. By SAFEnet's count, 5,549 digital rights violations were recorded from 2025 to mid-2026, a figure we could not check against any independent source. On 23 October, a legal team formed by SAFEnet with a journalists' association, legal aid groups and others opened a desk to hear from people whose content has been restricted. The restrictions apply inside Indonesia, and readers elsewhere are not directly affected.

According to SAFEnet's report, it and the media monitoring group Remotivi recorded at least 73 pieces of content taken down between April and September 2026, most of them criticising the president, the free nutritious meals programme or disaster response. A separate SAFEnet statement of 5 October gives the period as April to August, and says 90.4% were moderated or removed at the request of the Ministry of Communication and Digital Affairs (Komdigi). According to the same statement, the notices platforms sent on the ministry's request never stated which law had been broken. We found no public response from Komdigi to the figures of 73 items and 90.4%.

The National Commission on Human Rights (Komnas HAM) questioned Komdigi after receiving complaints of "internet restrictions" and "social media restrictions" during protests. On 13 October a commissioner relayed Komdigi's account that it removed 486 pieces of suspected illegal content, based on its online patrols, on 27 August, the day of large-scale protests. Komdigi also denied that it restricted the internet. The commission is still examining the legal basis for those removals.

Komdigi's own figures show about 4.2 million pieces of illegal content removed between October 2024 and April 2026, mostly online gambling and pornography. These are the ministry's own numbers, which we also could not check independently. The 486, the 4.2 million and SAFEnet's 73 are three different counts and cannot be added together or compared.

In mid-October, public figures said their posts about forest fires were reaching fewer people. Komdigi's deputy minister and then the minister denied that the ministry had asked platforms to remove or restrict information about the fires. In a video statement on 21 October, the minister also said the ministry is pushing for accountability and transparency in platform algorithms, and asked users to appeal to the platform first and then report to the ministry.

The legal team has not said in its press release what it would sue over or in which court. According to the release, filling in the form does not make someone a plaintiff, and that the choice of plaintiffs depends on evidence, harm and standing (whether a person is entitled to bring the case). The team also asks people to include screenshots of moderation notices from the platform, links to the content, and their correspondence with the platform.

Perspective

Ministerial Decree 127/2026, signed by Komdigi in March, classifies disinformation and hate speech as content that causes public unrest, and requires platforms to carry out an access cut-off order from the minister within four hours of receiving it. We could not find the decree itself, so its content here follows Kontan's quotations. According to the director for digital space control interviewed by Kontan, reported content is first reviewed jointly with the relevant ministries and agencies. Objections to the government are filed by the platform through SAMAN (the system the ministry uses to send orders to platforms and track compliance), and the ministry separately encourages platforms to offer users a way to object.

The ministry's reasons are set out in the considerations of the decree: disinformation and hate speech can cause public unrest, panic and conflict between groups. Before the decree was issued, the director general of digital space supervision also said in September 2025, when discussing SAMAN, that takedowns are not meant to silence criticism. In April, the Alliance of Independent Journalists (AJI) called for the decree to be revoked, arguing that terms like "causing public unrest" are too vague.

According to a commentary published by the University of Melbourne's Indonesia research outlet, a March Instagram post by the independent outlet Magdalene, which introduced an investigative report on an acid attack, was restricted inside Indonesia under this decree and the restriction was lifted a few days later. The commentary quotes the director general as saying the post's narrative and title could mislead the public and trigger distrust of state institutions, and that Magdalene is not on the Press Council's list of verified outlets. A Press Council member said Magdalene is a legitimate news organisation and that Press Council verification is not a legal requirement.

In its ruling of 29 September (311/PUU-XXIV/2026), the Constitutional Court declared the provision of the Electronic Information and Transactions Law that authorises the government to cut off access conditionally unconstitutional: the government must first issue a digital or written notice with reasons before it cuts off access or orders a platform to do so. The court did not accept the petitioners' argument that prior court approval should be required. As of 29 October, we had not obtained any public statement from Komdigi on the ruling, and found nothing on whether it has changed how it gives notice. SAFEnet calls the ruling a first step towards reform, and argues that because the ministry is both regulator and enforcer, notice alone does not guarantee that restrictions are proportionate.

OONI (Open Observatory of Network Interference, censorship measurements run by volunteers in many countries) and Cloudflare Radar (traffic monitoring) measure whether websites can be reached and overall traffic, so the removal of a single post or a drop in reach does not show up in their data. OONI's website connectivity measurements show no spike in anomalies on 27 August, and Radar has no outage annotation for Indonesia from late August to early September (checked on 29 October). OONI's coverage depends on where volunteers are and is uneven across telecom operators, so regional or operator-level interference cannot be ruled out.

For people whose content has been restricted or removed by a platform in Indonesia, the minister's suggested route is to appeal to the platform first and then report to the ministry. Keeping screenshots of notices and links to the content gives a basis for any later appeal or request for legal help (our suggestion, drawing on the types of evidence the legal team lists).

We are a community based in Taiwan. Elsewhere in Asia, who can order content removed and whether a court is involved are settled differently. In Thailand, the urgent procedure in a notification published in July has officials petition a court, with evidence, to suspend dissemination or remove online data.

In Taiwan, Article 46 of the Protection of Children and Youths Welfare and Rights Act requires platforms, once the competent authority notifies them that content is harmful to children, to restrict children's access to it or take it down. The notice goes to the platform, the article sets out no court procedure, and its scope is limited to child protection.

In Hong Kong, Schedule 4 of the Implementation Rules for Article 43 of the Law of the People's Republic of China on Safeguarding National Security in the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (2020) lets the Commissioner of Police, with the approval of the Secretary for Security, authorise a designated officer to act on electronic messages likely to constitute an offence endangering national security. The officer may require the person who published a message to remove it by a deadline, or require the platform to take a disabling action (removing the message or restricting access to it). If the platform fails to comply or that is not practicable, the requirement can go to a hosting service provider, and failing that, a network service provider. The rules do not require a court first.

Under the same rules, the publisher may receive a removal requirement directly and in writing, but Schedule 4 contains no provision on giving the publisher reasons or a route of appeal. Indonesia's ministerial decree and access cut-off provision let an executive body give orders directly, as in Taiwan and Hong Kong, while Thailand has officials go to a court. The Constitutional Court has now added prior notice with reasons.

When comparing approaches, it helps to ask who can order content removed, whether a court is involved, and whether the person affected receives a notice with reasons and can object. The intended effect of the policy belongs in the comparison too: whether there are published figures to test how well it is curbing disinformation, gambling and pornography.
